extracted.intended_audience: journalists, students of political science, and readers interested in media, public opinion, and democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging how newspapers serve democratic society — including their informational competence, economic incentives, independence, and role in making the 'invisible environment' visible to citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the invisible environment visible
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must report the world so that 'the realities of public life stand out sharply against self-centered opinion'; the truth about distant or complex matters is not self-evident and 'the machinery for assembling information is technical and expensive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil liberties alone do not guarantee public opinion on complex matters; institutions and education for reporting are required. Evaluators should ask whether a news organization has the resources, techniques, and institutional arrangements to render remote and complex affairs intelligible to citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech/civil liberties are necessary but insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic civil liberties (free speech, open encounter of opinions) are of great practical value but they assume truth is spontaneous or that means for securing truth exist without technical reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While defending free expression is essential, assessors should not assume that freedom alone produces accurate public opinion — examine the presence of technical reporting, education, and institutions that actively produce truth about complex affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic model: circulation sold to advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is an asset chiefly because it can be sold to the advertiser; the public generally does not pay directly for the full costs of newsgathering and thus the paper's economics are dependent on advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how funding and revenue models shape editorial choices. Consider whether the paper relies on concealed payments (advertising) and how that affects priorities and resource allocation for reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/advertiser match (quality vs mass circulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The kind of circulation an advertiser will buy depends on what he has to sell; it may be 'quality' or 'mass' circulation. Newspapers reaching the fairly prosperous (discretionary consumers) are most valuable to many advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a paper's audience demographic aligns with advertisers' target customers; this alignment will influence the paper's content, tone, and selection of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the buying public's point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A press that must be capitalized by turning readers into circulation sellable to manufacturers will 'respect the point of view of the buying public' — newspapers are edited for the buying public because without that support a paper cannot live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine editorial slant and topic emphasis for evidence of catering to the purchasing habits, tastes, or political views of the economically important readership segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty (constancy) as the principal source of independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper that can depend upon the loyalty of its readers is 'as independent as a newspaper can be' given modern economics; loyal readership can break up advertiser pressure and is more powerful than any single advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reader engagement and loyalty (subscription stability, repeat readership). Greater loyalty and a broad, devoted readership confer greater editorial independence from advertisers and special interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers' influence vs plurality of readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the number of advertisers and the broader the readership, the less influence an individual advertiser can exert; conversely, alienating the buying public makes a paper vulnerable to advertiser pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the concentration of advertiser revenue and whether editorial decisions appear to favor major advertisers. Check for instances where publishers 'betray' readers for advertisers and whether that stems from shared views or fear of losing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central role of key metropolitan dailies and press associations
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small number of metropolitan 'key papers' collect general news and supply many other papers (rural and special press) through press associations; for international news the national press may depend on a few metropolitan services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the news ecosystem: which outlets serve as primary gatherers, how reliant are other publications on those services, and how that centralization affects diversity and accuracy of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch between ethical expectation and economic reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The public judges newspapers by ethical standards (like church or school) expecting disinterested truth, but newspapers operate under market pressures and are often effectively given away to readers while supported via advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a paper, take into account this normative tension: the expectation of disinterested service versus the incentives created by subsidized pricing and advertiser funding that shape content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for standards of living and audit methods to control exercise of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Because political decisions are often invisible to ordinary citizens, democratic control depends on 'devising standards of living and methods of audit by which the acts of public officials and industrial directors are measured' and 'insisting that all of them shall be plainly recorded, and their results objectively measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a newspaper provides the factual record, metrics, and continual auditing/reporting necessary to measure governmental and industrial performance — not merely opinion or rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as the means to educate beyond self-centered opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinions of local groups about their wider rights and duties 'are matters of education or propaganda, not the automatic product of shop-consciousness'; therefore press reporting/education must stretch minds beyond direct experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether reporting helps readers form informed judgments about matters outside their immediate experience (contextualization, explanation journalism, sustained coverage) rather than merely reflecting parochial or self-centered views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized class and information asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex societies, governance often falls to a specialized class acting on information that is not common property; without proper reporting the public cannot hold that class accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which a newspaper reduces information asymmetries by making relevant expert knowledge accessible, thereby enabling public oversight of specialized actors.
